When old hardware is designed on FPGA, is that what is done? I mean, are designers making a copy of how a system functions down on the hardware level, and not making a duplicate of how it was originally designed? I suppose it probably depends on the project.

Adam
It does depend on what you are doing...

For example, the entire PDP 11 mini-computer was has been recreated in VHDL and can be put into many different FPGA development boards...
http://www.heeltoe.com/download/pdp11/README.html

If you treat the design you are recreating as a black box, you can simulate all the functions, you don't have to do it the same way as the original design. All that matters is simulating the function itself.

This is how MAME works. They did not duplicate the original games, just their functions.

For example, the Bally's 'Magic' write function. You don't need to know what it is doing in hardware, you just need to know what function it does, and then duplicated the result.

Old game systems are easy to duplicate. Many emulators have been written for game consoles.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_game_console_emulators

In the same way you can emulate the old systems in software, you can also emulate them in hardware.

The bally arcade would be a rather simple project to recreate in an FPGA. In fact, a quick search turned up this:
https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Astrocade_MiSTer

Someone already did it.

And I believe I've seen others comment that there is VHDL code for the bally arcade.

By the way, this triggered another thought... When a Bally arcade dies because one of the Bally 40 pin custom chips dies, there is a pace you can get more of those chips... Old stand up arcade game boards. If you can find old game boards for Bally arcade games, they use the same chips. So if an arcade game stops working for some reason, the chips may still be usable... Just a thought.

Some Bally Arcade/Astrocade Diagnostic Tips
By Michael Matte
June 7, 2020

Overview

This document isn't a how-to or a FAQ: it's a document created based on information exchanged via a few emails, phone calls and pictures between Michael Matte, Adam Trionfo, Ken Lill and Allen Schweitzer in May/June 2020.  Michael's final email response has some good information on troubleshooting the Astrocade.  Some of this information might be a bit out of context without the original emails, yet I decided to ask Michael if I could post his information, as it might prove helpful to some people who are having issues with fixing their Astrocade consoles or just want a little background on some of the different revisions of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade motherboards.  I hope that Michael's information will prove useful to Astrocade trouble-shooters.  I've included Michael's original email in-full here.  - Adam


From: Michael Matte
Sent: Sunday, June 7, 2020 1:55 PM
To: Adam Trionfo
Subject: Revised Follow Up To Allen Schweitzer

I expanded a few comments to the original follow up to Allen. You can post either version. Thanks.


This is my follow-up to your photo/info you emailed me on your four 2K ROM board and also when we teamed up over the phone to diagnose one of your failed motherboards.

The following are comments/questions related (or not) to the above statement.

I found a data sheet for the MK4096N-15 DRAM chip in Mostek's 1977 Memory Products Catalog. The maximum rating for the VDD supply voltage is 15.75V. The chip's access time is 350ns. In 1977, there were 12V 4096 chips and surprisingly 4027 chips available. No 4015 was listed in the catalog. I'm guessing, the -15 chip was used because it was the cheapest. The -15 chip was not listed in Mostek's 1979 data manual.

I have 2 working motherboards with the white ROM package. Both of these boards utilize 4015N DRAM. One white ROM displays a 1977 menu and the other white ROM displays the 1978 menu.

Any idea why the early motherboards utilized a plastic shield? Did the FCC later change the RF shield requirement to metal?

The Bally schematic in the Bally Service Manual PA- 1 shows the 26 point (double-sided) and 10 point (double-sided) diagnostic test ports (plug-ins) using a diamond symbol, pin number and test port designation. An example is ? pin 23 (26) shown at pin 15 of U20.

Thanks for sending me those photos of your four 2K ROM board. Do you have a close-up photo of the DRAM, the power supply and the front view of the +15V voltage regulator. If so, please email me them to complete my photo gallery of this rare motherboard. Thanks.

You can reduce the size of your computer photos to just fit your own personal monitor by using Windows Paint Program. This will save you a bunch of memory bytes. You can also add text notes to your photos. My HP monitor resolution can only display up to 1600 x 900 pixels max. Even with my Canon camera set at 1920 x 1280 pixels (2.5M), I still reduce my photo size to just fit my monitor, which typically requires only under 500K bytes for a photo.

I don't know how Windows reduces a hi-res camera photo to fit a monitor. Depending on the maximum pixel resolution your monitor can display, you might lose some fine detail in the Windows reduction. Whether there will be further loss of detail trimming down your camera photo using Windows Paint is unknown to me at this time. You could compare the normal Windows reduction with your Paint trimmed photo. Then decide if you really want to delete the actual hi-res camera photo file.

Do those custom chips on your four 2K ROM motherboards have small square metallic heatsinks? Allen's photos of the custom chips on his early four 2K ROM motherboard reveal some very distinct artistic 40 pin packages. The 40 chip pins look goldplated. The top of the package depicts the physical internal wiring to the chip core. The square shaped labels on the top center of the packages had some depth to it. I thought it might be a small metallic heatsink. Allen said it is not a heatsink.

The first test Balcheck performs is a RAM check, but this particular test only checks RAM locations 4F00-4FFFH (only 256 bytes) because the next check is for functioning screen interrupts, which requires a working Z80 stack area in RAM to execute a screen interrupt routine. Then Balcheck tests all of RAM. See the standard Balcheck tests in the BalcheckHR user manual for test details.

All 4 ROMs on the motherboard are wired identically on the motherboard. Based on Ken's info related to the four 2K ROM internal addressed decoding, the memory allocation for each 2K ROM chip is indicated below.

8K ROM select 0000-1FFFH
with chip internal address decoding
Label  A12  A11
HVSA     0       0
HVSC     0       1
HVSB     1       0
HVSD     1       1

HVSA  U4  0000-07FFH
HVSC  U2  0800-0FFFH
HVSB  U3  1000-17FFH
HVSD  U1  1800-1FFFH
Operating System      0000-0E18H
3 Games, Scribbling   0E19-1FFFH

Motherboard Locations
HVSD U1      HVSB U3
HVSC U2      HVSA U4

A BalcheckHR dual 7-segment display note.
A lowercase b is used to represent the hex digit B.
The lowercase b looks similar to the hex digit 6.
Don't confuse b with 6 on the 7-segment display.
A lowercase d is used to represent the hex digit D.
The BalcheckHR user manual warns the user of this possible misread.

BalcheckHR overlay
The BalcheckHR user manual is written assuming an overlay is utilized. Buy and cut to size, some general-purpose stick on labels. Attach labels to the Scribbling or spare Astrobasic overlay and relabel. See the user manual for details.

The Nutting Manual has some general info within its "System Description" which would likely help you diagnose a failed motherboard. There is also info in the BalcheckHR user manual related to troubleshooting. Both manuals are archived on the Bally Alley.

SetScreen3 has an option to "Halt" the Z80 CPU, which might help your diagnosis when using a logic analyzer. When a Z80 Halts, it just executes NOPs. See SetScreen3 in the BalcheckHR user manual for details.
There are also 2 troubleshooting loops. See the "Optional Troubleshooting Programs" in the BalcheckHR user manual.

I did document a procedure for checking all 8 rectifier diodes for an "open" or "shorted" diode, without desoldering any diode leads. See my article in the Bally Alley FAQS section "Troubleshooting The Power Supply In The Bally/Astrocade Home Computer System". The procedure is described in the last paragraph of the section labeled "Full Wave Rectifiers", which begins on page 2.

Next time you replace more than one RAM chip on a motherboard, please document any RAM error report before and after the chip replacement, plus the chip number that was replaced, so we can determine if any false reports were displayed. Thanks.

I am likely going to write a commentary for the Balcheck RAM error report code 04. The commentary would cover topics such as listed below.
What is Balcheck really telling me with the code 04 report?
How does Balcheck test the 8 RAM chips?
Is every RAM byte tested?
How is a RAM error saved and reported?
How are the screen RAM bits mapped?
What exactly does each RAM chip store, screen bytes or pixel bits?
Why does Balcheck sometimes display inconsistent or bad reports?

End of follow-up

Bye.

On June 27, 2020, Michael Matte replied, privately, to me (Adam) about this RGB upgrade and he said:

"Adam, when you had in the past powered on the Astrocade menu using a TV, did you ever see a narrow vertical colored stripe to the right of the Menu display? I have and that occurrence may be typical on TVs. I found out that the stripe is a result of the data chip's horizontal color boundary (used to split the TV screen in half for extra colors) being set just a tad short by 1 byte. I made an internal ROM adjustment, moving the boundary 1 byte to the right, on my "Remote ROM" scheme, which is part of the BalcheckHR package. That minor adjustment eliminated the vertical stripe to the right of the Menu display.

"As crayon king progresses through his/her project, he/she might find out that a narrow vertical stripe on the right of the menu display might not be removable by electronics. The complete elimination might require an adjustment to the horizontal color boundary in the ROM program. I believe you also see this striped occurrence in Seawolf."

Bye.

Actually, studio analog video using the BetaCam format was pristine. (Not to be confused with the Betamax ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betamax ) format )
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betacam
The analog video recording quality of BetaCam when played back could not be distinguished from a live camera (if everything was calibrated correctly... 😉)
BetaCam used the "Y", " R-Y", "B-Y" component format for recording the signal. And it was amazing.

Also, analog HD recorders were even higher quality. I'd have to see the signals side by side, but an old Analog HD analog signal would probably still look better than today's digital 4K signal. You would be surprised at how good an analog recording could be if done right.
https://www.broadcaststore.com/store/model_detail.cfm?id=666647
But the early Analog HD formats were not compatible with the current ATSC digital HD formats. The early analog format only had 1035 lines. Later digital formats used 1080 lines.
The early Analog HD format used a 30 MHz bandwidth, instead of the current 6 MHz bandwidth. That meant that the analog signal had amazing high frequency detail.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_high-definition_television_system

But, digital has one advantage over analog.
That is, you can make copy after copy after copy of a digital signal, and all generations will look as good as the 1st generation.
Unfortunately, only the first generation of an analog recording looked the best. Just like making a copy of a copy on a Xerox machine, making analog copies degraded the signal with each copy. And after just a few copies you could tell the difference between the original and the copies.

I still have old analog HD video tapes in my garage. Just nothing to play them on... 😔

MCM Design is pleased to announce the completion of its 8KB hi-res Multi-Pager Test Demo package. In September 2019, MCM Design announced a design breakthrough with a new modified for hi-res Astrocade prototype. The prototype's hi-res screen RAM operates using only 4 static RAM (SRAM) chips, instead of the normal 32 DRAM chips. This breakthrough announcement is posted on the Bally Alley website.

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html

Scroll down to "MCM Design Hi-Res Static Ram Announcement".

Each SRAM chip stores 32KB, providing a 4 chip total of 128KB of screen RAM. A variation of the Datamax UV-1R multi-pager was added to the new prototype allowing user selectable access of up to 8 pages of 16KB hi-res screen RAM, mapping 320 x 204 pixels per page.

The hi-res map is described in the Nutting Manual system description, pages 85 and 87. This manual is archived on the Bally Alley website.

The multi-pager includes a provision for an additional 8 pages (128KB) of screen RAM.

The 8KB Multi-Pager Test Demo package is detailed below.

Features:

The 8KB Test Demo resides as a cartridge ROM program at 2000-3FFFH.
All necessary hi-res routines reside within the test demo program package.
No user RAM above 8000H is required to run the package.
A standard low-res ROM (or custom 8KB ROM at 0000-1FFFH) is required only to jump to the test demo at 2000H.

A normal system reset executes in sequence the following:

1. Multi-pager 8 page flip test
2. A program which moves a critter around all 8 pages to erase each page's static graphics
3. Hi-res 7 color Fish Demo

This 3 part sequence can repeat nonstop.

An optional 4th program is executable by holding down any key in the right-most keypad column, while pressing the system reset button. This program allows a viewer to move a critter, using a hand controller at the #1 controller input, around within 3 connecting scenes (pages). The 3 scenes have simplified static graphics.

The hi-res Fish Demo can be run independently on a modified hi-res Astrocade with NO multi-pager by holding down any key in the left-most keypad column, while pressing the system reset button. The hi-res screen map must be compatible as described in the Nutting Manual mentioned above.

The vertical blanking line is dropped to the very bottom of the screen RAM area in all 8 pages so the viewer can observe a 98 byte program copied into page 7 plus observe the stack area being worked by the Z80 CPU in all 8 pages.

202 lines of the available 204 horizontal screen lines are utilized for screen graphics in all 8 pages.

Multi-Pager 8 Page Flip Test

The multi-pager's operation is tested to see if all 8 pages of graphics can be written to perfectly by visually watching for graphic errors while the pages are flipped automatically. All 8 pages are written with static graphics as indicated below.

Page                      Hi-Res Graphics Written

   0                           text introduction
                                with 17 lines of custom 7 x 9 pixel text characters

   1                           fill narrow vertical stripes on a split screen

   2                           end view of aquarium plus 15 magic write variations

   3                           fill narrow horizontal stripes on a split screen

   4                           10 color textured graphics pattern

   5                           fill narrow vertical plus horizontal stripes on a split screen

   6                           multi-pager title page
                                with custom enlarged text characters

   7                          custom hi-res screen shot variation of the game Gunfight

While the text intro is being displayed, the remaining 7 pages are written with static graphics as described above. The viewer is given nearly 60 seconds to read the 3 paragraph intro. There is an option to skip the intro by holding down any key on the keypad, which reduces the read delay time to about 5 seconds. Seven pages must be written first before the flip to page 1 will occur automatically.

There are 5 passes of page flipping. Each pass flips through the 8 pages faster. The 5th pass flips about 3 pages per second. An audio flip sound is output during each page flip. The multi-pager handles (selects) the page to flip by a simple output to the custom port 74H. After the 5 passes are completed, the next program in sequence is executed.

Move Critter Within All 8 Pages

A 98 byte program is copied from the ROM cartridge program package to page 7 beginning at address 7F20H. This program in page 7 is then executed to move a critter around the screen in all 8 pages, to erase all or most of the static graphics. The program in page 7 utilizes subroutines within the test demo package.

This test program was created to see if the multi-pager could function perfectly, loading a machine language program into a specific page, then execute that program moving a graphic pattern around in all 8 pages. Special attention was necessary to point the Z80 CPU to a specific page, for any screen RAM writes or reads, by using the multi-pager's custom output port 75H. This attention included pointing to a specific page to work any Z80 stack areas, variables, flags and data blocks within a page's scratchpad area.

The critter's initial appearance location in each page is randomized to appear anywhere along the screen's X axis or Y axis.

After the critter is finished with the last page 7, the hi-res Fish Demo is then executed.

Hi-Res Fish Demo

Twelve fish using 5 fish types swim around the screen. One fish likes to linger along the sea bottom.

The initial locations of 11 fish are randomized. The fish lingering along the sea bottom likes to appear near the center top of the sea bottom.

A  ML routine was created to flop left a fish pattern facing right within the same pattern frame by adjusting the pattern frame's X coordinate. In this demo, bit 7 within a magic register value is used as a flag for a custom request to adjust the X coordinate for a flop. Bit 6 is the flag that actually requests a magic flop. Bit 7 in the magic register output port is not utilized by the Astrocade's magic hardware to request any specific magic function, so this bit is available for a programmer to flag the execution of a custom ML routine related to a magic function.

Two screen interrupt routines are used to provide 7 different colors. One of the screen interrupt routines also updates a hr:min:sec elapsed time clock (up to 9:59:59).

The elapsed time utilizes custom hi-res 7 x 9 pixel digits. A custom display time write subroutine was created to write the time digits (and colons) using an expanded plop with NO shifter byte cleared at the end of each digit line written. This may be the reason why the timer counts up with NO graphics flickering.

When the elapsed time reaches 2:00 minutes, the fish demo will execute a restart (jump) to 2000H to start over again the execution of the multi-pager test demo. This restart cycle will repeat nonstop.

The fish demo will run nonstop if any key on the keypad is pressed before the 2:00 minute restart time expires. An up arrow will be displayed to the right of the elapsed timer to indicate the fish demo nonstop mode was enabled. The fish demo runs in page 0.

This fish demo utilizes an expanded version of Andy Guevara's clever programming technique to move multiple fish around a screen using only one vector block in the RAM scratchpad. MCM Design expanded the same technique to include multiple types of fish.



Cycle Time

The cycle time from start to finish, executing the multi-pager flip test, moving a critter to erase static graphics in all 8 pages plus the 2:00 minute fish demo, is about 9 minutes. This cycle time includes the text intro 60 second read delay.



Final Note

Out of curiosity, MCM Design ran the Multi-Pager Test Demo on its original modified hi-res Astrocade, which utilizes the 32 chip DRAM scheme and has no multi-pager.

You can view a portion of the Multi-Pager Test Demo on a modified hi-res Astrocade having NO multi-pager. You will briefly see the normal text intro followed quickly by 7 variations of the remaining 7 page writes, ending with the Gunfight screenshot.

If you press a key or wait out the 60 second read delay, you will see the Gunfight screenshot going thru multiple color changes and you will hear the flip page sound with each change. The changes along with the flip sound will also speed up. Then the program will crash, sometimes forcing a system reset to occur. You do however get a really long look at the hi-res Gunfight screenshot going through multiple color changes, which is a pretty cool graphics variation. This screenshot has the best graphics of the 8 pages displayed normally.

So, whether or not a hi-res Astrocade has a multi-pager, you still get to see some pretty cool hi-res graphics with this 8KB hi-res package.



End Of MCM Design Announcement
June 2020

Try this kludge.  I bet it fixes the problem.

Back in October of 2019, I posted a video that provided a background and pictures created on the Astrocade by Video Wizards in 1982.  Ken Springsteen (the guy behind Video Wizards) drew the pictures.  Yesterday he posted a comment on the video on YouTube.  Ken said:

"Thanks for posting this.  When Montgomery Ward's started selling the Bally Arcade I volunteered to do in-store demos of the Bally Basic. This led to helping people I had met, in the store, at their homes. The algebra that had made no sense to me in high school now had some practical application that was revealed through many long nights of trial & error punching in Bally Basic with that little keypad overlay. When ColecoVision came out, I moved on. First there was a concept & design that I submitted to Rob Fulop (creator of Demon Attack) @ Imagic. Though it generated some interest, it was never fully developed. Then an idea that I submitted to MicroLab, with full concept description & artwork, led to a 3 year contract to do original concept & design work. Around one year in, the videogame industry experienced the infamous falling out. MicroLab went bankrupt. I continued to go to the CES in Chicago to meet with companies when Nintendo first released the NES. The software development was all based in Japan & they expressed no interest in accepting submissions from the U.S.  I noticed that several elements of the Super Mario game were very similar to ideas I created back in the days of ColecoVision. Probably just a coincedence! Through all this, I kept my "day job" as a printer & have enjoyed 41 years in the industry, so far."

If you're interested in watching the video, then you can see the link in my original message (below).

Note that no program called "Graphic Pictures" was released on tape.  Rather, Ken Springsteen, the programmer, had an unusual method of distributing his software along with the six programs that he wrote:

1) Jekyl & Hyde
2) Multi-Graphics
3) Crypt-O-Grams
4) The Exterminator
5) Slow Machine
6) Lazer Brains

These eleven pictures have been gathered into one video for easy reference and viewing.  The graphic programs do allow the graphics to be changed by the user with, as Paul Thacker (who archived these programs) describes it, "a rather cumbersome interface."  The method to change the graphics is not shown here, nor are any BASIC program listings for the programs.

The video is broken down into several sections:

0:00 - Overview of Video Wizards and Graphic Pictures

The following are the eleven pictures in this video

7:19 - Welcome to the World of Video Wizards
7:53 - Thank You for Ordering Software from Video Wizards
8:16 - Charlie (The Man of 1,000 Faces)
8:39 - Arcadian Logo

9:34 - Space Creatures

12:04 - End Credits

The video has a 1/2 page newspaper advertisement for the Astrocade with the Z-GRASS unit.  This is from the Winnipeg Free Press's October 9, 1982 issue.  There are three other ads from the Arcadian.

Ken Springsteen, the man who programmed these graphics, left the Astrocade scene by around June 1982, when he put up his collection for sale.  This means his "company," Video Wizards, was only in business for three to four months.

The UltiMulti uses a third-party cartridge shell.  It's pretty common for them to not quite fit into the unit all of the way.  When this happens, then the games don't work and the Astrocade acts as though there is no cartridge inserted at all.  Whenever I use my UltiMulti, I have to wedge a piece of folded-up, thick piece of paper between the front of the cartridge and the front of the place where the cartridge is inserted into the Astrocade.  Try this kludge.  I bet it fixes the problem.

Adam

Lance has suggested-- and it sounds reasonable to me-- that the early Astrocade consoles shipped with whatever dust covers were on-hand at Astrovision, Inc. That's a clever logo; it's SO cleaver, in fact, that I didn't get it on my own.  I cropped a close-up of the Bally dustcover and added the words "Fun & Brains" to make the connection more obvious to people who need help, like me, making the connection between the logo and the catch-phrase.

I've created a video overview of the "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program" which allows a user to load a Bally BASIC program saved in 300-baud format onto the Bally Arcade/Astrocade "AstroBASIC" cartridge using that cartridges built-in 2000-baud interface; no 300-baud external interface is required.  Once the program is loaded into "AstroBASIC," then it can be modified (if desired) and then saved in 2000-baud format.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=snNI2Piiyvc
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/snNI2Piiyvc/maxresdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=snNI2Piiyvc>
300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program by Jay Fenton Overview Astrocade AstroBASIC 1981<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=snNI2Piiyvc>
300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program By Jay Fenton For the Bally Arcade/Astrocade and Astrocade BASIC "AstroBASIC" Manual, Appendix F, Pages 104-107...
www.youtube.com
This video overview may only be for those interested in archiving Astrocade tapes.  The audience is small, but for those who might appriciate this video, I'd like some feedback.  This program probably never had too many users... but am I the ONLY one who uses this programs in the 21st century?

"AstroBASIC" has a special command for loading machine language programs directly into screen memory, bypassing the BASIC language format entirely.  It is called "COLON-RUN," and is typed in similar to the familiar :INPUT command.  RESET your computer and type:

:RUN

The TAPE CONVERTER PROGRAM loads using the :RUN command.  When loaded, the screen background brightness will change continuously.  Cue up the 300 baud tape, press GO, and load the 300 baud program into the computer.  Observe the program statements accumulating in the buffer just below the program zone.  The screen will reveal the scratchpad during this phase.

Program loading will stop on any of the following conditions:

(a) :RETURN is found in an unnumbered line.
(b) RUN is found in an unnumbered line.
(c) Any other key in the column beneath HALT is pressed.

Cases (a) and (c) will cause the program to go back to the flashing grey scale mode.  Case (b) will cause the program to proceed to final loading.  If you wind up in the grey scale mode and have no more segments to load, press HALT to get to the final loading.  After HALT is pressed, or RUN is found, the program will convert the statements in the buffer into the representation used within your Bally BASIC.  This is done by moving the buffer to the highest possible address and using special I/O routines which feed characters from this buffer to the Bally BASIC Input routines.  This will be seen on the screen as a race between the input buffer and the program storage area.  The CONVERTER PROGRAM will then exit to Bally BASIC.  The variables A to Z will be zeroed out, and the screen will be cleared.  The program may now be executed or written out at
2000 baud.

I have added a gameplay video, along with a slight overview, of the expansion RAM version of the game Pack-Rat.  The original version is by WaveMakers for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade; it was released for Bally BASIC in 1980 and AstroBASIC is about 1981 or 1982.  This version loads via the 300-baud interface and was released in about 1984.

The code between the two versions of the game is very different, as the version for Expanded BASIC takes advantage of new BASIC commands like SNAP, SHOW, PLAY and DATA.  However, the only obvious difference between the original version of the game and the newer version are the game's graphics: the old version uses squares to represent a mouse and a cat.  Pack-Rat for Expanded BASIC has a "Pac-Man" (for the mouse) and a "ghost" (for the cat).

This version has been converted to use Expanded BASIC by WaveMakers or, since this version may not have an official release (as there doesn't appear to be any advertising for it), it could have been modified by someone else and passed around the Astrocade community. If anyone here is following my YouTube channel (BallyAlley, of course) then you've seen that I've been playing around with my long-mothballed Amiga computers-- indeed I plan to upload a video that focuses on my Amiga 2000 today.  I still have plenty of Atari computers and (again, of course, Astrocade consoles), but when my C64 died many years ago, I was burned trying to replace it with a NOS PAL motherboard.  That sort of soured me on the scene.

To bring this back around to the Astrocade, I'll mention that Mike White was among the few people who had an EPROM burner for his Astrocade.  Here are some pictures of it:

https://ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/eprom_burner/eprom_burner.html

You'll notice that his Astrocade is sitting on top of... something.  I'm pretty sure that is his 64K RAM board.  I wish I had a better camera back then for higher quality pictures or even a video or two, but these pictures were taken at the CCAG show in 2001:

https://www.ccagshow.com/

If you browse around the BallyAlley website, then you'll find some information on EPROM burners, plus Astrocade software that allows you to use them.  All that being said, I'd rather use an EPROM burner for a modern computer, if it supports the older chips.  They work MUCH fast and there are many advantages to them.

Oh, and Tom, thanks for reminding me about the DuckDuckGo search engine.

Adam

17363:
here is the programming info for the mcm68764. A 2764 will be the same, with the same pinout, The 27C74 will work but requires 12-12.6 VPP voltage and a diffefent timing.
MCM68764, MCM68A764 PROGRAMMING INSTRUCTIONS After the completion of an ERASE operation, every bit in the device is in the "1" state (represented by Output High). Data are entered by programming zeros (Output Low) into the required bits. The words are addressed the same way as in the READ operation. A programmed "0" can only be changed to a "1" by ultra-violet light erasure. To set the memory up for Program Mode, the E/Vpp input (Pin 20) should be between +2.0 and +6.0 V, which will tristate the outputs and allow data to be set-up on the DQ terminals. The VCC voltage is the same as for the Read operation. Only "a's" will be programmed when "a's" and" 1 's" are entered in the 8-bit data word. After address and data setup, 25 volt programming pulse (V,H to V,HP) is applied to the E/Vpp input. A program pulse is appl ied to each address location to be programmed. Locations may' be programmed indivi-dually, sequentially, or at random. The maximum pro-gram pulse width is 55 ms and the maximum program pulse amplitude is 26.0 V. Multiple MCM68764s may be programmed in parallel by connecting like inputs and applying the program pulse to the E/Vpp inputs. Different data may be pro' grammed into multiple MCM68764s connected in paral-lel by selectively applying the programming pulse only to the MCM68764s to be programmed

Yep. I was not a fan of FORTH, and especially not a fan of terse FORTH. And the hardware was the DataMax UV-1 development system.
The higher level language was suppose to allow the programmer to leverage high level routines to make coding easier.
But the higher the level routines you used, the more overhead it took. And it made doing certain things fast harder.
My personal style of coding was just to code directly in Z80.
And my own development system that we created was more powerful in debugging (in my opinion).
So when they wanted me to use Terse FORTH to program in, they actually were hobbling my programming skills...
17370:
So all of the info on this system came from Jamie Fenton.  Most of it is
archived here:
http://www.bitsavers.org/pdf/nuttingAssoc/icebox/

Someone else got it booting in MAME, and I helped a little to get the disk
emulation working.

It's been a couple years since I used it. For now, I can describe the
screenshot a bit.

I don't know if this latest version of the ICEBOX could boot CP/M.  I
booted Terse Forth in my screenshot session.
I believe the disk image in my screenshot is the one with the production
Gorf arcade image on it.

To get a disk to boot, you hit Ctrl-C from the % prompt.  This disk had
Terse on it.

As far as I can tell, at that point you have an extremely minimal support.
Namely, you can load more from the disk.
To get more, I typed "220 LOAD" which loads more Terse from block 220 on
that disk.
(The scanned disk label from this disk reads"220 LOAD")

At that point, I have enough Forth that I can create a simple 1-line Forth
program TEST.  You can see it prints numbers.

Finally the DIR command prints the first line of each block, containing an
ASCII header, from a range of blocks on the disk.

Note that all the operands come before the commands, "220 LOAD", "180 181
DIR" - it's Forth!

The original system would be connected to Arcade hardware or an Astrocade
console, via a ribbon cable.
You load code into RAM, which was in the memory map of the target, and run
it, breakpoint, single step, etc.
Unfortunately. the emulation doesn't support that "joined" configuration
right now.  You can load code into RAM but it doesn't do anything.

There is a lot more that came with the system, including manuals, and disk
images.

Next steps would be...
- To sort out more of what can be done with the OS and Application disks.
- Setup a combo MAME driver with the icebox+astrocade or icebox+gorf, etc.
- Finish reverse-engineering the schematics for the Icebox from the photos
on bitsavers. (Someone started but got busy)

I'd like to see all that happen in the future. If someone with the skills
wants to run with it, please contact me and I will help get you started.

-Frank

"H-10 - Misc. Art" is a collection of miscellaneous video art written for Blue Ram BASIC.  According to the BASIC listing, this program is called:

3K PROG. H-10 MISC. ART

"H-10" was found in Ken Lill's tape collection.  As far as the program's archiver, Paul Thacker, knows, "H-10 - Misc. Art" was never published.

This program presents a menu with the following options:

1 - Expanding Circles
2 - Circle Art
3 - RND Disappearing Lines
4 - Edit / M.W.S Program
5 - Circles?
6 - Square Circles
7 - Box Formation - Boxes
8 - Box Formation - Circles
9 - Unusual Circles

The description for options 4, "Edit" refers it having been originally written by Michael White.

Eight of the nine options run as expected, but Option 5, "Circles?" doesn't work.

Starting @ the pin fartherst away from the line filter, the pins are numbered 1-8.
pin1) Video varies depending on what is on the screen.pin2) +10V acuarate by +/- 1.0 Volt MAXIMUM (Typically 0.5V)
pin3) Audio also varies, but dependant on the sounds being generatedPin4) Chroma This pin has the signal that defines the actual color. It is actually          over 3MHz continuosly, just changing phase angle.pin5) is +2.5V this is generated by the Custom DATA chip. If this voltage is off, 
         this could be your problem. Acuracy +/- 0.25V
pins 6&7) These are your video information. (R-Y & B-Y) Yhey, too, vary per          screen.
Pin 8 is -5V Thyis also mut be acurate by +/- 0.5V
Pins 2,5 and 8 are your power supply voltages. They need to be as close to acurate as possible.To check the others, you will need something like an oscilliscope.
As far as the LM1889 chip, Pin 14 s/b 10V, pin 5 s/b -5V and pin3 s/b 2.5V
If these voltages are correct, then I would say there is a probably a circuitry problem, like a short on the PCB.

17425:
Something to keep in mind about all video upgrades that ditch RF is that these games were meant to be played on color televisions from the 1970s/early 1980s era.  You'll find that you'll see some significant color changes across various consoles when an upgrade is installed.  I've seen it myself on the Astrocade.

Probably the worst victim of a too-much-video upgrade is the Atari 8-bit home computers.  Even the original Atari 800-- out of the box-- could display s-video (back then, I believe it was called luma/chroma).  But... if you use S-video, then you lose all the color in games that take advantage of "artifact color."  (Side-note: I THINK that the trick used to make color on the Apple II is something related to color artifacting).

I don't think that you'll lose color on any astrocade games, but there are many, probably several hundred, games on the Atari 8-bit that become black and white-only affairs with s-video.  For me, I prefer composite-out on 8-bit systems, s-video-out and analog RGB-RGB on 16-bit era systems and, on later systems, I like component.  Am I missing any of the analog output methods on classic game systems and computers?

All this said, if we don't play the systems we own, like if they're kept on a shelf and never brought out and hooked-up, then the best TV/monitor image doesn't do any of us any good at all.  Here's what I say: plug in the nasty, smeared, wavy color-shifting, dot-crawling, RF-out signal from your Astrocade and Atari consoles and get busy playing a game; that's the best way to enjoy our classic systems.  Let's get cracking!

Adam

I took a look at the power supply schematic in the Bally Service Manual. Cap C8 is at the input of VR1, VR2 and VR3. Cap C8 is also in parallel with the 1500uf cap C1. Cap C1 is intended to reduce the DC rectifier ripple at the VR1 thru VR3 inputs. Note there is also a 0.1uf cap at the inputs of VR1 and VR2, which are used to pass certain undesirable DC transients to gnd instead of passing through the VR. I'm speculating that cap C8 is sized NEAR the desired capacitance to pass a specific transient (or range of transients) to gnd instead of the 3 VRs, The output of VR3 is fed into the sensitive base of transistor Q1. Increasing the cap breakdown voltage rating of a cap slightly will likely just change it's physical size, but one should also pay attention to the cap's capacitance tolerance, which may affect the cap's performance in a particular circuit if the tolerance is too high. In the Bally Service Manual, the 100uf cap C10 is rated at 16V. I've been running a 100uf cap rated 35v on both of my modified hi-res motherboards for many hours. If this higher rated cap is creating an issue on my motherboards, I haven't seen the issue.  

If you have an oscilloscope, you could temporarily experiment with a 22uf C8 connecting the scope at the +5VDC line along with a DC voltmeter. Then momentarily, run nearby a 120VAC power drill or paper shredder checking for transients on the scope or a major change in the DC voltage. Check the TV display or audio output and note any undesirable changes/interference. Run the same test with a 6.8uf cap. Keep in mind that a motor may generate RF interference.  Otherwise, if you really want to know, you're forced to research power supply design bypass capacitor criteria (yuck!) or consult with someone knowledgeable in this particular application to determine if there is a high risk of damage due to DC transients for any of the motherboard chips by tripling the capacitance of C8.

Anyway, the above is my opinion, for what is worth.

Bye.
MCM

Thanks for the photos. Are you talking about a glue that permanently attaches a heat sink to a chip? How well does that glue transfer heat from chip to heat sink? Is that glue designed for that application? Have you experimented with silicone grease? I found that silicone grease tends to harden a little with age making it harder for the heat sink to slide off a chip. One use to be able to buy black finned heat sinks specifically designed for 40 pin chips. Silicone grease would be a better choice for a deluxe heat sink, because the heat sink would be removable. I'm curious, if you are just going to attach a piece of metal, how well does that application work when the motherboard is run for an extended time with its console cover in place? 

As a reminder, MCM Design highly recommends:

1. Always run the motherboard with the console cover off and using a small 6 inch fan to keep the custom data chip and power supply heat sinks cooler.

2. Protect the primary side of that black power transformer from gnd or near gnd shorts by splicing in a standard  1 1/4" in-line fuse covered holder to a small extension cord. You might be able to go as low as a 1/2A (500mA) SFE fast acting fuse to help protect the XFMR. Jameco sells this type of holder.

3. Power on the power transformer and motherboard simultaneously using a power strip, leaving the motherboard power slide switch in the "on" position. The motherboard power switch does NOT shut down the entire motherboard power supply. Shutting off power using a power strip also discharges the motherboard 10,000 uf cap faster.

4. Finally, as you know, replace at least the original aged power supply caps 10,000uf C6, 1500uf C1 and 100uf C10. Cap C6 must be rated higher than 10V. Using a cap with a higher capacitance is ok and will reduce the DC ripple some, which is good.

I took a look at the power supply schematic in the Bally Service Manual. Cap C8 is at the input of VR1, VR2 and VR3. Cap C8 is also in parallel with the 1500uf cap C1. Cap C1 is intended to reduce the DC rectifier ripple at the VR1 thru VR3 inputs. Note there is also a 0.1uf cap at the inputs of VR1 and VR2, which are used to pass certain undesirable DC transients to gnd instead of passing through the VR. I'm speculating that cap C8 is sized NEAR the desired capacitance to pass a specific transient (or range of transients) to gnd instead of the 3 VRs, The output of VR3 is fed into the sensitive base of transistor Q1. Increasing the cap breakdown voltage rating of a cap slightly will likely just change it's physical size, but one should also pay attention to the cap's capacitance tolerance, which may affect the cap's performance in a particular circuit if the tolerance is too high. In the Bally Service Manual, the 100uf cap C10 is rated at 16V. I've been running a 100uf cap rated 35v on both of my modified hi-res motherboards for many hours. If this higher rated cap is creating an issue on my motherboards, I haven't seen the issue.

If you have an oscilloscope, you could temporarily experiment with a 22uf C8 connecting the scope at the +5VDC line along with a DC voltmeter. Then momentarily, run nearby a 120VAC power drill or paper shredder checking for transients on the scope or a major change in the DC voltage. Check the TV display or audio output and note any undesirable changes/interference. Run the same test with a 6.8uf cap. Keep in mind that a motor may generate RF interference.  Otherwise, if you really want to know, you're forced to research power supply design bypass capacitor criteria (yuck!) or consult with someone knowledgeable in this particular application to determine if there is a high risk of damage due to DC transients for any of the motherboard chips by tripling the capacitance of C8.

Anyway, the above is my opinion, for what is worth.

Bye.
MCM

Is that glue designed for that application? Have you experimented with silicone grease? I found that silicone grease tends to harden a little with age making it harder for the heat sink to slide off a chip. One use to be able to buy black finned heat sinks specifically designed for 40 pin chips. Silicone grease would be a better choice for a deluxe heat sink, because the heat sink would be removable. I'm curious, if you are just going to attach a piece of metal, how well does that application work when the motherboard is run for an extended time with its console cover in place? 

As a reminder, MCM Design highly recommends:

1. Always run the motherboard with the console cover off and using a small 6 inch fan to keep the custom data chip and power supply heat sinks cooler.

2. Protect the primary side of that black power transformer from gnd or near gnd shorts by splicing in a standard  1 1/4" in-line fuse covered holder to a small extension cord. You might be able to go as low as a 1/2A (500mA) SFE fast acting fuse to help protect the XFMR. Jameco sells this type of holder.

3. Power on the power transformer and motherboard simultaneously using a power strip, leaving the motherboard power slide switch in the "on" position. The motherboard power switch does NOT shut down the entire motherboard power supply. Shutting off power using a power strip also discharges the motherboard 10,000 uf cap faster.

4. Finally, as you know, replace at least the original aged power supply caps 10,000uf C6, 1500uf C1 and 100uf C10. Cap C6 must be rated higher than 10V. Using a cap with a higher capacitance is ok and will reduce the DC ripple some, which is good.


Bye.
MCM

Never leave a console from any generation prior to the PSX on when not in use. If you are turning off a power strip and leaving a console on, you are still risking a static discharge damaging the unit when you power back up, even with a surge protected power strip. If you are going to leave multiple consoles plugged in when not in use:
1. Invest in a good surge protector to reduce "noise".2. Make sure you have a modern, grounded wall plug for the surge protector.3. As a secondary cut off, have a licensed electrician install a wall switch for the wall plug. This gives you a double terminal cutoff when not in use and protects electronics in the event of something like a lightning strike. Grounding your wall plug is extremely important!

17493:
We were trying to include many more things in the second release (we were allowed to include the Vectrex ROMs in the first release since it was a not-for-profit release), but rights turned out to be a quagmire.  One of the problems was figuring out who had the rights to begin with, and/or if the rights were free and clear for the primary holder to assign rights to others.  One person I spoke with put it pretty plainly that the only way it could be resolved would require a lot of legal fees, and wouldn’t get done unless we wanted to pay for it all.  Yeah...  What little profit we actually eked out would not have covered more than an hour of one clerk’s time digging out paperwork, let alone actual lawyers sorting out what that paperwork meant.  So, some of the rights we were looking for remain absolutely unsorted.  Luckily, Atari and Bridgestone at the time had sorted out *their* stuff, so we knew for free what we could or could not get ahold of.  Even then, Atari balked at a number of things, because the $1 a disc royalty we paid wasn’t enough for even the uncertainty other potential licensees might see in their properties despite the paperwork saying we had only a limited use for them, and they could license too.

Russ

We were trying to include many more things in the second release (we were allowed to include the Vectrex ROMs in the first release since it was a not-for-profit release), but rights turned out to be a quagmire.  One of the problems was figuring out who had the rights to begin with, and/or if the rights were free and clear for the primary holder to assign rights to others.  One person I spoke with put it pretty plainly that the only way it could be resolved would require a lot of legal fees, and wouldn’t get done unless we wanted to pay for it all.  Yeah...  What little profit we actually eked out would not have covered more than an hour of one clerk’s time digging out paperwork, let alone actual lawyers sorting out what that paperwork meant.  So, some of the rights we were looking for remain absolutely unsorted.  Luckily, Atari and Bridgestone at the time had sorted out *their* stuff, so we knew for free what we could or could not get ahold of.  Even then, Atari balked at a number of things, because the $1 a disc royalty we paid wasn’t enough for even the uncertainty other potential licensees might see in their properties despite the paperwork saying we had only a limited use for them, and they could license too.

Russ
